Chapter 2: Breaking Down Barriers and Building a New Culture
Imagine stepping into a leadership role at a massive organization. It’s a bit like walking into a maze, isn’t it? There are layers of management, those endless meetings, and a culture where being cautious seems to slow even the best ideas to a crawl. For someone who’s always thrived on action and real results, this kind of environment can feel downright stifling. You feel that urge to shake things up growing stronger every day.
The real taste of leadership came with a promotion—taking charge of a small but talented division. But here’s the thing: the team was weighed down by old habits and a real fear of making mistakes. You could see it in the way people held back, worried they might step on someone’s toes or draw the wrong kind of attention. That’s when the new leader decided it was time for something different.
Instead of sticking to the usual hierarchy, the focus shifted to open conversations and honest feedback. Everyone was encouraged to speak up, to challenge assumptions, and to bring their best ideas to the table—no matter where they sat on the org chart.
One of the first big changes? Cutting through those layers of management that slowed everything down. Meetings became shorter, sharper, and way more focused. Decisions started happening faster. The message was clear: speed matters, and bureaucracy just doesn’t have a place if you want to win. Sure, this approach ruffled a few feathers—especially with people who were comfortable with the old ways—but it also energized the team. People started stepping up, taking more initiative. And before long, the results spoke for themselves.
There was a defining moment when the division faced a tough call—a struggling product line was dragging the business down. The numbers were clear: this wasn’t working. So, instead of dragging out the process or sugarcoating the truth, the leader gathered everyone together and laid out the facts. The conversation was honest, sometimes even uncomfortable, but it led to a clear decision: it was time to cut losses and move on. That moment reinforced just how important candor is—and how making tough calls can actually be the best thing for the entire team.
As the division started to turn things around, word spread across the company. Other teams began to notice—and even adopt—a similar approach. Suddenly, a new culture was taking root. People stopped worrying about protecting their own turf and started working together across boundaries. Sharing ideas, collaborating, even being rewarded for helping others succeed, not just for hitting their own goals. The idea of “boundaryless behavior” caught on and started breaking down those old silos, sparking real innovation.
Through all these changes, one thing became crystal clear: culture isn’t built on policies or catchy slogans. It’s shaped by what we do every day—and by how willing we are to challenge the status quo. When people feel empowered to speak up, to take risks, and to push for better, the whole organization moves faster and achieves more. The shift from a rigid, hierarchical company to a dynamic, collaborative one was just getting started. But the foundation was set: candor, speed, and a relentless focus on results.
